newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC pledges to curb excess supply; oil market unconvinced.
newsitem.headline: OPEC pledges to curb excess supply; oil market unconvinced.

text.p: OPEC delegates ended their talks Thursday with a new freeze on oil production, but the latest attempt to convince oil markets that the cartel can shore up a dilapidated quota system appears set to backfire.
Prices jumped higher initially on word Wednesday that the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries had struck a deal to "roll over" the current output ceiling to year's end.
More important was the agreement that OPEC nations would stop producing in excess of their quotas.
But on Thursday, prices retreated, just as the group formally endorsed the deal. In late trading on the New York Mercantile Exchange, August crude oil was off 40 cents at $19.12 a barrel.
Analysts said that over the long term, the market would demand proof of what OPEC said were fresh promises that mandated quotas would be honoured.
Saudi Arabia and Iran put their authority to the test at the Vienna meeting. They joined forces to put pressure on others among the 11 members who are violating oil output limits.
Oil Minister Ali Naimi of Saudi Arabia said there was "100 percent commitment" among member countries.
Such alleged violators as Venezuela and Nigeria were said by sources to have acknowledged, under Saudi Arabian and Iranian pressure, that they were over-producing.
The OPEC accord puts a ceiling on OPEC output at 25.03 million barrels a day, including Iraq's sales under its food-for-oil deal with the United Nations.
But industry monitors say that violations of individual quotas have taken actual supply to 27 million bpd.
Prices have sagged this year from $25 in January to the current level of $19.
Acccording to a Gulf source, Venezuela admitted that it produced 800,000 barrels, or 30 percent more than its quota during a candid session of ministerial talks.
"What is new is the complete honesty. All of the cheaters made confessions," said the source.
Some analysts said they doubted that the quota deal would hold together.
OPEC's problem is that it lacks a mechanism to compel a sovereign state to honour its quotas.
"It's a fantasy world. The quota system is a mechanism for losing their share of the market," said Geoff Pyne, analyst at UBS.

OPEC's biggest producers remain hopeful that quotas can be used to push oil prices higher. But analysts say the sceptical oil market is likely to wait in vain for firm evidence that wayward over-producers honour their commitments.
"People will not believe that anything has changed until they see it," said Leo Drollas, economist at former Saudi Oil Minister Zaki Yamani's Centre for Global Energy Studies.
